title: 7-Eleven Japan has a “Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet” that’s fiery red… but how hot is it?
description: Spoiler alert: Your taste buds aren’t ready for this convenience store katsu. One of the great things about convenience stores is their wide variety of hot food, giving us a simple way to pick up a snack that’s easy to eat while on the go. Not all the hot food is that easy to eat, […]
content:
Spoiler alert: Your taste buds aren’t ready for this convenience store katsu.

One of the great things about convenience stores is their wide variety of hot food, giving us a simple way to pick up a snack that’s easy to eat while on the go. Not all the hot food is that easy to eat, though, as we recently found out when we stumbled upon 7-Eleven’s “Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet”, which practically burnt the taste buds off our tongue with a level of spiciness we weren’t expecting.

Things started off easy, as we spotted the fried cutlet in the hot food display and were instantly drawn to its fiery red appearance. As ardent spice lovers who’ve rarely been challenged by self-proclaimed “super spicy” products before, we casually picked one up to find out how mild it would be, but when we took a bite we immediately swallowed our pride.

From that very first bite, it felt like a flame had been ignited on the tip of our tongue, and the fire quickly spread to cover the entire palate, burning with an intensity that never let up. Surprisingly, it wasn’t just the fried coating that delivered the spicy hit, as the heat came from inside the minced-meat filling as well, giving us double the burn, for twice as long.

▼ Amidst the pain, our taste buds battled against the heat to assess the flavour, because for us, that’s the true marker for a really good hot product.

As it turns out, the flavour was one of the highlights – the filling contained a generous amount of juicy meat, with garlic chives adding an extra element of taste to make the whole thing even more delicious. Perhaps because of the minced meat and garlic chives, the cutlet had a vaguely gyoza-like flavour. Either way, both the taste and the heat were excellent, especially when combined with the wonderfully crispy coating, which crunched satisfyingly between the teeth with every bite.

▼ However, there was one thing that eluded us: what exactly makes it “Taiwan”?

We weren’t sure what the “Taiwan” in “Taiwan Mince Cutlet” was referring to, but after checking 7-Eleven Japan’s official site, we learned that the filling is “Taiwan Minchi” (“Taiwan Mince”) a spicy seasoned minced meat originating in Nagoya. So, in the end, the “Taiwan” in the name refers to the spicy and savoury minced meat filling used in dishes like Taiwan ramen from Nagoya’s famous Misen restaurant.

That’s also why it’s called a “minchi cutlet” rather than “menchi katsu”, which is the usual term for a Japanese-style minced-meat cutlet. It’s also the reason why the filling contains garlic chives, which you don’t normally find in a Japanese-style menchi katsu.

What started out as a chance encounter turned into an exciting journey of discovery, as we not only found out that the cutlet was hotter than any other convenience-store hot food we can remember trying, but also that its name pays homage to the “Taiwan” mince associated with Nagoya’s famed local food culture.

Priced at 189 yen (US$1.18), the Super Spicy! Taiwan Mince Cutlet really does live up to its name, so be sure to stop by your local 7-Eleven soon if you’re game enough to try it, as it’s only available for a limited time.

title: Study finds hundreds of people in Indonesia legally named after Naruto, Inuyasha, other anime stars
description: Anime’s growing international popularity is affecting name choices overseas. content:
Anime’s growing international popularity is affecting name choices overseas.

Popular storytelling tropes and traditions mean there’s often a degree of overlap among anime protagonists, but the characters that leave the deepest impressions tend to bring their traits together in some singular way that makes them stand out from the pack. So while, for example, anime has plenty of hot-blooded martial artist heroes, there’s only one Naruto, right?

Except, actually, in Indonesia, there are well over 100 Narutos. And no, this isn’t the result of somehow amplifying the power of bunshin/shadow cloning techniques, but part of a trend of actual people in Indonesia having the name of anime characters.

Earlier this month, Indonesia’s Directorate General of Population and Civil Registration (a.k.a. Dukcapil), part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, released its latest census data and found a surprising number of residents whose names clearly come from the anime/manga world. The most common anime name among the people of Indonesia is Uzumaki, with 190 people using Naruto’s surname as their name, while another 157 Indonesian residents are named Naruto. Hailing from the same series, the Dukcapil found 158 Sasukes and 152 Uchihas, creating totals of 347 people who owe their name to “Naruto Uzumaki” and 310 to “Sasuke Uchiha.” The census also turned up 60 people named after Boruto, Naruto’s son and star of his own sequel spinoff.

Doraemon also had a strong showing for inspiring names, with 181 people named Nobita, after the series’ lead human character. There are also 16 people in Indonesia named Doraemon, and another 8 share the name of Nobita’s wealthy associate Suneo.

Pirate saga One Piece’s popularity has resulted in 79 people named Luffy and 37 named Usopp. 65 people are named Shinchan, as in the titular tyke of Crayon Shin-chan, and Indonesia is also home to 23 people named Inuyasha.

To be clear, these tallies aren’t for people who use the anime character names as a professional name, nickname, or alias. The census counted official, legally registered names, meaning that any passports, driver’s licenses, or other official forms of ID issued to these people really will list their name as “Naruto” or “Inuyasha.”

The publicly released census data doesn’t seem to account for whether or not the people with these names are native Indonesians, but it’s unlikely that many of them are ethnically Japanese foreign residents. Naruto isn’t really a name that’s used in Japan, and Uzumaki is an incredibly rare family name, with estimates that there are fewer than a dozen Uzumakis in all of Japan. Sasuke is an actual given name, but one that’s very old-fashioned (we’re talking “immediately calls up images of ninja from hundreds of years ago” old-fashioned), and Uchiha doesn’t appear to be an actual surname name. The closest name out of those listed above that you’d be likely find an actual Japanese person with would be “Shin,” but even then, no Japanese person would make the affectionately diminutive suffix “-chan” part of their legal name.

Taking all that into consideration, it appears that these names really are the result of anime’s popularity in Indonesia, and with the medium’s global fanbase continuing to grow, we might be seeing even more anime names in the real world in years to come.

Source: Jiji, Yomiuri Shimbun, International Business Times, Myoji Yurai.net (1, 2)

title: Pokémon donuts are coming to Krispy Kreme in the U.S. [Photos]
description: Pikachu, the original starter trio, and one more old-school Pokémon are getting ready to warm fans’ hearts and satisfy your sweet cravings. We recently found out that McDonald’s is going to be offering Happy Meals with crossover Hello Kitty/Godzilla figures later this month at its branches in the U.S., and while we’re obviously happy that […]
content:
Pikachu, the original starter trio, and one more old-school Pokémon are getting ready to warm fans’ hearts and satisfy your sweet cravings.

We recently found out that McDonald’s is going to be offering Happy Meals with crossover Hello Kitty/Godzilla figures later this month at its branches in the U.S., and while we’re obviously happy that people will have their burger and adorable toy needs covered, there is still one critical culinary component missing: dessert. Thankfully, after having your appetite whetted for adorable Japanese pop culture tie-ins, you can continue right on to Krispy Kreme, which has revealed that it’ll soon start selling Pokémon donuts in the U.S.

Offered as part of the ongoing 30th anniversary celebration of the Pokémon franchise, Krispy Kreme will be baking up a half-dozen different themed treats, starting with, naturally, a Pikachu donut featuring vanilla icing and a lemon cream filling.

All three of the Gen 1 starters are here too, Bulbasaur’s donut is the simplest, essentially one of Krispy Kreme’s flagship Original Glazed donuts enhanced with colorful vanilla icing and “leaves” made of frosting.

The Charmander donut gets caramel icing and a toasted marshmallow filling as a nod to the Fire-type’s powers.

Squirtle’s is the most elaborate-looking of the three starters’ donuts, with a swirl of cotton candy-flavor buttercream and sanding sugar.

The above-listed quartet often serve as ambassadors for the Pokémon franchise as a whole, and when there’s room for one more in a collection, the nod often goes to Eevee or whichever Pocket Monster species is having a moment, like Snorlax or Ditto are right now with their prominent roles in Pokémon Sleep and Pokémon Pokopia. However, Krispy Kreme has instead recruited Jigglypuff, who serves as the inspiration for a strawberry buttercream-topped donut with strawberry cookie crumbles.

Finally, rounding out the lineup of a half-dozen Pokémon donuts is an Original Glazed cosplaying as a Poké Ball thanks to vanilla and chocolate icing plus a whole bunch of crimson sprinkles.

Each of the species-specific Pokémon donuts also comes with a little paper decoration of its associated Pokémon. They’ll also be gracing the cups of Krispy Kreme’s donut holes…

…and Pokémon-theming will be showing up on Krispy Kreme boxes as well.

Krispy Kreme’s Pokémon donuts go on sale in the U.S. on August 18, the exact same day as McDonald’s Sanrio/kaiju Happy Meals.

title: 12-year-old foreign tourist missing in Japan, police asking for help finding her [Video]
description: U.K. middle schooler seen on security camera footage after leaving family’s rental property alone. Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old middle school student from the U.K., arrived in Japan for sightseeing with her parents and older brother on July 21. She has now been reported missing, and the police are asking for help in finding her. […]
content:
U.K. middle schooler seen on security camera footage after leaving family’s rental property alone.

Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old middle school student from the U.K., arrived in Japan for sightseeing with her parents and older brother on July 21. She has now been reported missing, and the police are asking for help in finding her.

The Paul family is currently staying at a private rental property in Tokyo’s Kamata neighborhood. The last time the family saw Carmelita was on the night of August 12, when her father spoke with her before going to bed. When the rest of the family woke up at around 8:30 on August 13, she was gone.

▼ Video showing a photo of Carmelita released by the police as part of the call for help locating her

Carmelita did not take a phone with her when she left, so the family had no way of contacting her. The family contacted the police shortly before 9:30. In examining surveillance camera recordings the police found images of Carmelita, dressed in a sky-blue sleeveless top, black-and-white checked skirt and black pumps, and carrying a pink handbag, walking in the Nichome section of Kamata, near the family’s rental property. Investigators were able to determine that she passed through Yokohama Station, roughly 20 minutes south by train from Kamata Station, later that same morning, but have been unable to trace her path any farther than that.

Carmelita did not take her passport with her when she left the rental property, and her family estimates she had only a few thousand yen (less than US$100) on her, which would not be enough for an extended stay in reputable lodgings. The Tokyo/Yokohama area has also been experiencing severe rain showers , making proper shelter even more important than it would usually be.

The police describe Carmelita as being roughly 160 centimeters (5 feet, 3 inches) in height, with a medium build and curly black hair. Anyone with information as to her whereabouts is asked to contact the Tokyo Metropolitan Police’s Kamata Station at the phone number 03-3731-0110, but information can also be submitted at any police box or station.

title: Google’s first Google Store outside the U.S. is now open in Tokyo
description: But it’s not in electronics neighborhood Akihabara that Google has chosen to set up shop. Omotesando, the tree-lined boulevard that stretches out from the corner of Harajuku Station in downtown Tokyo, has been a mecca for fashionistas for generations. Now, though, it also boasts a new attraction for tech fans, with the opening of the […]
content:
But it’s not in electronics neighborhood Akihabara that Google has chosen to set up shop.

Omotesando, the tree-lined boulevard that stretches out from the corner of Harajuku Station in downtown Tokyo, has been a mecca for fashionistas for generations. Now, though, it also boasts a new attraction for tech fans, with the opening of the first-ever Google Store outside the U.S.

Google Store Omotesando held its grand opening on August 13, welcoming visitors to come in and get hands-on looks at its Google Pixel smartphone line. The shop is also stocked with Fitbit, Nest, and other Google devices, as well as accessories such as Pixel cases from Tokyo-based manufacturer Casefinite.

There’s also a help desk with staff ready to answer questions, help resolve performance problems, or perform repairs for Google devices and services, and in-store pickup of items ordered online from the Google Store can be arranged too.

▼ Video of the Google Store Omotesando’s grand opening ceremony on August 13

One could make the argument that, what with Japan still having a relatively robust brick-and-mortar shopping sector with large-scale physical electronic stores staffed with knowledgeable salespeople, Google doesn’t need its own dedicated store to help with distribution, sales, and after-service. The primary benefits that Google is hoping for with its first store in Japan, though, can probably be guessed through its choice of location. Google is likely hoping that by having a footprint in Omotesando, the neighborhood’s fashionable, sophisticated and cosmopolitan image will come to be associated with its products and services too. As a matter of fact, rival Apple has a store of its own about 10 minutes’ walk further down the street…

…and Samsung’s Galaxy smartphone brand has a Harajuku showroom that’s even closer.

Considering, though, that for many people in modern life the idea of going out without your phone is as unthinkable as going out without getting dressed, maybe it’s a natural evolution that Harajuku is becoming a place where clothing and smartphone brands alike feel they need to be.

title: Ride a tram that survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima on a new limited-time history tour
description: Step back in time on Hiroshima’s “Peace Loop 653”, a special tour that links passengers to the city’s past and present. Visitors to Hiroshima tend to have an interest in learning about its past, as it was one of only two cities, alongside Nagasaki, to have experienced an atomic bombing. Now, the city is offering […]
content:
Step back in time on Hiroshima’s “Peace Loop 653”, a special tour that links passengers to the city’s past and present.

Visitors to Hiroshima tend to have an interest in learning about its past, as it was one of only two cities, alongside Nagasaki, to have experienced an atomic bombing. Now, the city is offering visitors a unique way to connect to that history, as Hiroshima Electric Railway is running a limited-time sightseeing tour aboard the historic 653 tram, one of the few vehicles to survive the bombing of 6 August, 1945.

Called “Peace Loop 653”, the tour takes place on the tram, which was built in 1942 and was operating near Eba in Hiroshima when the atomic bomb was dropped. Although it was severely damaged, it was repaired and returned to service just four months later.

▼ Eba is around 3.4 kilometres (2 miles) from the Atomic Bomb Dome.

The tram continued operating for decades and is now preserved as a special event vehicle. While it occasionally runs for commemorative occasions and special events, the Peace Loop 653 tour gives visitors a rare opportunity to ride the historic vehicle as part of a guided tour.

▼ Restored to its original appearance, the tram even has a wooden interior that reflects the look of Hiroshima streetcars in the 1940s.

The Peace Loop 653 takes passengers around Hiroshima’s city centre on a loop route, circling around twice as onboard commentary introduces passengers to the city’s history, recovery, and modern attractions.

The tour departs from Hiroshima Station, where passengers are welcomed by a guide wearing a restored 1940s-style uniform. Before boarding, participants will receive a special souvenir inspired by wartime-era tickets, adding another element of history to the journey.

On the first loop of the tour, passengers learn about Hiroshima before the atomic bombing and in the immediate aftermath. Historical footage from the era will be available to watch on tablets during the ride, allowing visitors to see how the city looked before and after the bombing.

The second loop around focuses on Hiroshima’s recovery and its present-day identity. Using an original tour map, passengers can discover the city’s rebuilt streets, local attractions, and recommendations from guides. During this part of the journey, passengers who prefer to hop off before Hiroshima Station can do so at select stops, although once passengers disembark from the tram it will conclude their tour as they won’t be able to reboard.

▼ First loop in purple, second loop in navy, with stops for alighting in yellow and Hiroshima Station in the red box.

The route above is read as follows:

Loop 1: Hiroshima Station – Inari-machi – Kamiyacho-higashi – Hondori – Takanobashi – Hiroden-honsha-mae – Minami-machi rokuchome

Loop 2: Minami-machi rokuchome – Matoba-cho (alighting stop) – Hatchobori (alighting stop) – Hondori (alighting stop) – Hiroden-honsha-mae (alighting stop) – Hijiyama-shita (alighting stop) – Hiroshima Station (final stop)

▼ The tram utilises the purple loop route, and a portion of the light green route, seen on the upper right.

The tour also includes a two-day Hiroshima Tabi Pass, which gives participants unlimited travel on select local trains, buses, and other transport services during their stay. The experience lasts around 40 minutes from Hiroshima to the first alighting stop, or 90 minutes for the full two-loop journey to and from Hiroshima Station.

Each tour is limited to 25 passengers, with morning and afternoon departures on select weekends and public holidays. The 10:30 a.m. morning departures will take place on 5, 6, 19, 20, 21, 22 September and 10, 12, 24, 25, 31 October. The 1:30 p.m. afternoon departures will take place on 19, 20, 21, 22 September.

▼ Take a look at the Peace Loop 653 service below.

Tickets cost 3,500 yen (US$21.96) for adults (junior high school age and above), 1,500 yen for elementary school-age children, while preschool children ride free. Advance reservations are recommended (online bookings here), but if seats remain available, same-day applications will also be accepted at Hiroshima Station.

Being able to ride a tram that survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima is a rare experience that connects you to the city’s past in a truly tangible and memorable way. Not only is it a reminder of the city’s war-torn past, it’s also a symbol of survival that’s symbolic of the city itself, and you can ride the tram during its limited run until 31 October.

title: Watch a sumo bout inside Tokyo Tower, at a new restaurant endorsed by two yokozuna
description: Sumo and chanko nabe are just some of the highlights of this new Japanese culture experience. Despite its worldwide fame, not a lot of people actually get to watch sumo. Not only are tickets incredibly hard to get – the official site is so busy when sales start that it’s virtually impossible to access and […]
content:
Sumo and chanko nabe are just some of the highlights of this new Japanese culture experience.

Despite its worldwide fame, not a lot of people actually get to watch sumo. Not only are tickets incredibly hard to get – the official site is so busy when sales start that it’s virtually impossible to access and everything sells out within minutes – but tournaments are only held during very limited periods at certain locations each year, which might not match up with the time and place of your visit.

Now, though, there’s a convenient way to get a taste of the sport, thanks to a brand new restaurant experience called Tokyo Sumo Club Entertainment. After opening its first branch in Sapporo last summer, the restaurant is now coming to Tokyo due to popular demand.

▼  Located on the fifth floor of Tokyo Tower’s FootTown, the restaurant offers more than just sumo and a meal.

Every diner will get to enjoy a “Traditional Japanese Musical Instruments and Dance” performance, a procession by Oiran courtesans, a performance of a famous Kabuki play, and a festival with a lion dance and traditional music. There’ll also be a tradtional bon odori dance and mochi pounding, which guests can take part in.

▼ Learn about kabuki…

▼…and oiran.

At the centre of it all, though, is sumo, with visitors able to watch an entrance ceremony, practice sessions, and serious bouts. A salt-throwing experience and Q&A session is also included, as well as a “Challenge Sumo” experience where you can wrestle with a sumo wrestler.

The venue contains a real clay sumo ring, with diners seated around the ring in a way that mimics the seating at a real tournament venue.

While other sumo restaurants exist in Tokyo, this one is unique in that it’s said to be the only one in Japan officially endorsed by two yokozuna: the 63rd Yokozuna Asahifuji and the 70th Yokozuna Harumafuji.

▼ Asahifuji speaking at the grand opening.

The endorsement of two sumo champions – yokozuna is the title given to the highest-ranking wrestlers – makes this a sumo experience like no other, and Asahifuji has even given his endorsement to the authentic chanko nabe (sumo stew) served at the restaurant. There are three dining options available, all of which include chanko nabe, differing according to seating tier.

▼ Standard

▼ VIP (different dish in the bottom right-hand section of the box)

▼ V-VIP

▼ A vegetarian option is also available upon request.

There are four performances each day, at 11 a.m., 2 p.m., 5 p.m. and 8 p.m., with each experience lasting around 90 minutes. The venue has 177 seats, and reservations can be made online, although walk-ins are also possible if seats are available.

Prices start at 12,000 yen (US$75.32) for children and 16,000 yen for adults in standard seats. VIP seats cost 14,000 yen for children and 20,000 yen for adults, while V-VIP costs 25,000 yen, regardless of age. Each plan includes all the performances, as well as a Japanese meal, one drink, a commemorative photo and a souvenir.

So if you’ve always wanted to see sumo firsthand but haven’t been able to secure tickets to one of Japan’s six annual tournaments, this might just be the next best thing. Not only is it much easier to book (tickets can be purchased here), but you also get to experience a number of other Japanese cultural events at the same time, and while you’re there you can cap off your visit with a trip up Tokyo Tower.

title: Krispy Kreme Japan is baking up two new donuts that you can only get at one spot in the country
description: Two classy fall flavors are on their way, but might require some travel to taste. We’re still in the middle of a very hot summer in Japan, but Krispy Kreme is already looking ahead to autumn, though not necessarily out of a desire for cooler weather. No, what they’re looking forward to is seasonal fall […]
content:
Two classy fall flavors are on their way, but might require some travel to taste.

We’re still in the middle of a very hot summer in Japan, but Krispy Kreme is already looking ahead to autumn, though not necessarily out of a desire for cooler weather. No, what they’re looking forward to is seasonal fall ingredients, with two fancy new donuts that you can only get at one Krispy Kreme branch in all of Japan.

Once again it’s Krispy Kreme Premium Nagoya, located inside the JR Nagoya Takashimaya department store near Nagoya Station, that’s baking up the exclusive treats. Earlier in the year this location began offering special lemon and peach donuts, but soon they’ll be shuffled off the menu to make room for the tastes of chestnut and fig.

The first of the two new donuts will be the Waguri An Butter. Pictured above, this is a fluffy donut with cream and an (sweet bean past) inside, both enhanced with the taste of waguri (“Japanese chestnut”). The cream and an will be sandwiched around a pat of butter, a nod to Nagoya’s penchant for pairing butter and an for a decadently rich sweetness.

Sweets fans across Japan eagerly await the annual wave of chestnut desserts that come out every fall, but debuting alongside the Waguri An Butter is another uniquely autumn flavor that doesn’t get as much confectionary representation.

The Fig and Black Tea Mont Blanc has the traditional ring donut shape, but its toppings are rather innovative. Sitting directly on top of the donut is black tea cream, presented in coils like the candied chestnut cream of a Mont Blanc dessert, and sprinkled with shredded Uba tea leaves. Swirled on top of the cream is a circle of fig jam, and altogether they promise a sophisticatedly complex mixture of sweet, astringent, and tart notes.

The Waguri An Butter and Fig and Black Tea Mont Blanc are identically priced at 389 yen (US$2.40) and both make their debut at Krispy Kreme Premium Nagoya on August 21, where they’re slated to be available through early December.

title: New Wet Rice Cracker Burger from Dom Dom breathes new life into a “miracle” snack
description: Snack that saved a Japanese railway gets a whole new look for a limited time. Japanese-born fast food chain Dom Dom Hamburger has a reputation for being edgier than most, with outrageous menu offerings that take things to extreme places other chains dare not go to. ▼ Now, Dom Dom is flexing its creative muscles […]
content:
Snack that saved a Japanese railway gets a whole new look for a limited time.

Japanese-born fast food chain Dom Dom Hamburger has a reputation for being edgier than most, with outrageous menu offerings that take things to extreme places other chains dare not go to.

▼ Now, Dom Dom is flexing its creative muscles yet again, with a new menu item called the “Nure Senbei Burger”

In all our years of eating fast food, we’ve never seen a burger like this. Instead of buns, it uses two pieces of “nure senbei” (“wet rice crackers”), a famous Japanese snack that Choshi Electric Railway, a local railway in Chiba, is particularly known for selling. As the name suggests, nure senbei differ from regular rice crackers in the sense that they’re delectably moist instead of crunchy, and they tend to be coated in a soy-sauce based glaze, making them a very left-field ingredient for a burger.

Dubbed a “miracle rice cracker”, as the struggling railway was able to survive through nure senbei sales after it began selling the snacks in 1995, Choshi Electric Railway’s variety comes in three flavours. Dom Dom doesn’t reveal which flavour of senbei is used in the new burger, though, so to solve that mystery, and find out what a wet rice cracker burger might taste like, we headed over to the Aeon Kaihin Makuhari branch to try it out.

It’s not easy to find the new burger, as the collaboration is limited to select stores in the Kanto region. Even at branches that do offer it, the promotional marketing tends to be kept to a minimum, as we found out at Aeon Kaihin Makuhari, where we only spotted a small mention of it on a laminated sign next to the till.

▼ New releases are usually advertised on giant banners outside this store, but this burger is only advertised on a small A4-sized poster near the register.

The burger is priced at 890 yen (US$5.93), or 1,290 yen as part of a set, and the ingredients are listed as: Two pieces of Choshi Electric Railway’s “nure senbei”, two meat patties, lettuce, cheddar cheese, a fried egg, special burger sauce and mayonnaise.

About five minutes after ordering the burger, our remote buzzer went off to tell us our order was ready, and we went off to collect the burger from staff. When we got back to our seat, we couldn’t stop looking at the “Nure Senbei” sticker on the packaging, which was a very weird sight for a burger, even of the Dom Dom kind.

▼ ぬれ煎餅 = Nure Senbei

We then unwrapped the burger to find…

▼ … a burger without bread buns!

The burger sat there staring back at us, with two wet rice crackers protecting its modesty, looking more like a couple of flat pancakes rather than senbei. Even though we’d read up on the burger and thought we knew what to expect, nothing could’ve prepared us for seeing the real thing right before our eyes.

▼ Curious to see what it contained, we lifted the nure senbei on top, and were surprised to find a large piece of…lettuce?

Nure senbei and lettuce aren’t two things you’d normally associate with each other, and neither is a fried egg, two meat patties, onions, and melted cheddar cheese, which were hiding out between the crackers.

▼ There was plenty of sauce on the bottom senbei too.

After inspecting the construction of the burger, we couldn’t help but be impressed at how well the senbei looked as a burger bun. However, after taking a knife to the burger, in an attempt to check the cross-section, we were surprised to find that the senbei totally resisted the pressure of the blade.

▼ The knife just wouldn’t cut through it at all.

Whereas a normal bun would give way easily, the nure senbei pushed the knife right back, reminding us of the strength of wet rice crackers, which aren’t easy to break apart. Determined not to be defeated, we persisted with the knife until we were able to somehow create a ragged cross-section, revealing it was much flatter than other Dom Dom burgers we’ve tried, which tend to be multi-layered feasts with a lot of height to them.

▼ After conducting our visual inspections, it was now time to get eating.

As soon as we bit into the burger, we knew this was going to be a very different fast food meal. The texture was unlike anything we’d ever experienced, with the nure senbei having just the right amount of moisture, soaking up the meat juices from the patties and the special burger sauce. The fragrant aroma of the soy sauce glaze was present in every bite, pairing perfectly with the egg, while the rich sauce added a mellow richness and the cheddar cheese brought everything together with a salty moreishness.

▼ It was way tastier than we ever thought it would be – who knew the meaty fusion of a burger and senbei could go together so well?

The burger was so good it didn’t take us long to devour it, but before polishing it off, we remembered we were here to solve the mystery of the nure senbei flavour. We’d come prepared with one of each flavour of the original senbei, purchased from the railway store before arriving, so we opened them up to try and identify which one was in the burger.

▼ Choshi Electric Railway’s nure senbei comes in three flavours: Red Rich Soy Sauce, Green Sweet, and Blue Light Soy Sauce.

So…which one of these was being used for the burger?

▼ Let’s start with the Red Rich Soy Sauce.

On its own, this senbei was incredibly delicious, but we held back on eating it all, instead taking small bites of it alongside the nure senbei used in the burger. Immediately, we could tell this one wasn’t it, as the aftertaste was stronger and obviously different.

▼ Next was Green Sweet.

The moment we popped this one in our mouth, we thought, “Could this be it?” It was very close, but after going back and forth between them several times, we started to sense that the aftertaste was subtly different.

▼ And finally, Blue Light Soy Sauce.

▼ Yep, this is it!

Or was it? Since we couldn’t completely rule out Green, we continued alternating between Green, Blue and the “Nure Senbei Burger” in small bites. This confused our taste buds even further, but in the end, we settled on the conclusion that for us, the Blue Light Soy Sauce was definitely the closest match.

▼ After this taste comparison, we also discovered another fun fact: the nure senbei used in the burger seemed to be slightly smaller than the standalone varieties.

This led us to believe that this nure senbei was likely to have been made specifically for the burger. As for the flavour, though, we ended up being right on the money, as the day after our visit, the chain announced that the flavour being used in the burgers was indeed Blue Light Soy Sauce.

The announcement gave us extra faith in our abilities as taste testers, and by our judgment, this is a burger that’s definitely worth trying. The creative concept behind the burger is matched by the skill used to execute it, creating a unique burger with a very Japanese twist that you won’t be able to enjoy anywhere else.

On sale from 10 August, the burger is only available at seven stores in the Kanto region listed below:

  • Kaihin-Makuhari Store
  • Higashi-Narashino Store
  • Ichihara Elephant Kingdom Store
  • Mobara FC Store
  • Noda-Ungapura Plaza Store
  • Aeon Style Akabane Store
  • Higashi-Ojima Store

Sure, other fast food chains might test the boundaries of the burger by swapping out buns for rice patties, but only Dom Dom could reach for a wet rice cracker and show us that it deserves a place in the burger world. Hopefully the chain will be able to somehow give it a permanent place on the menu so that Dom Dom fans in other areas will be able to discover the joys of a Wet Senbei Burger.

title: Japanese gacha machine in Shibuya now sells tiny capsule terrariums
description: We join the “koke katsu” trend to find out if these little ecosystems are as easy to make as they say. Japan is famous for its gacha machines, which dispense all sorts of products at random, through the clever use of capsules. After purchasing everything from tiny edible cakes to Casio Watch rings at these […]
content:
We join the “koke katsu” trend to find out if these little ecosystems are as easy to make as they say.

Japan is famous for its gacha machines, which dispense all sorts of products at random, through the clever use of capsules. After purchasing everything from tiny edible cakes to Casio Watch rings at these machines, we thought we’d seen everything we could possibly see…until the other day, when we stumbled upon a surprise find at Shibuya Hikarie in Tokyo.

After stopping by the building for lunch, we were initially drawn to a store on the fifth floor, which grabbed our attention with its rows and rows of what looked like aquariums from a distance.

Stepping closer, we found that the name of the store was “Terrariums Shibuya”, and that was exactly what it was selling. Terrariums enjoyed a bit of a boom in Japan when people were spending more time at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving rise to the term “koke katsu” (“moss hobby”) amongst enthusiasts.

With terrariums being essentially miniature ecosystems that need to be cared for, we’d always felt a bit too intimidated to take up the hobby, but here in this store we came across something that was perfect for newbies like us.

▼ A “Capsule Terrarium” gacha machine!

Now this seemed like something we might be able to manage. Small, cute and cheap – each turn of the machine cost 500 yen (US$3.33) – the “Feel the Garden” capsule terrariums contain everything you need to make a mossy terrarium, including the moss, an essential element.

▼ A cultivation kit for growing moss…all inside a gacha capsule.

After receiving our tiny gacha terrarium, we couldn’t resist spinning the handle on the machine beneath , which sold “Terrarium Figurine Gacha” for 300 yen.

Excited to find out what lay inside the capsules, we took them home and decided to start by opening the “Capsule Terrarium”. Inside, we found the following items: Moss, Waterproof Sticker, Terrarium Soil, Decorative stones, Decorative Sand (the sand and stone types are random to each capsule) , Tweezers, Dropper, Spoon, Pick , Fixing ring , Instructions.

We were honestly surprised by just how much had been packed into the little container. Of course, the capsule itself is an essential part of the setup, so we immediately got to work, following the included instructions and video link to set it up.

▼ The first step involved placing the waterproof sticker over the hole in the capsule, and then adding the terrarium soil.

After arranging the decorative stones in the sand and pushing them in slightly, we used the dropper to add water until the entire surface of the soil became dark brown.

Next, it was time to sprinkle in the decorative sand. According to the instructions, you’re supposed to sprinkle it in areas where you won’t be planting moss, and if you’re not sure where to put it, it’s recommended that you arrange it along the edges of the capsule.

▼ We added ours in bit by bit with the spoon.

Now it was time to plant the star of the show: the moss! It was dry when we took it out of the bag, but the instructions reassured us that this was totally fine – it was still alive, just in a dormant state.

▼ Once it absorbs water it resumes growing, so the dormant state is what makes it possible for a living thing like this to be sold in a gacha machine.

After tearing the dried moss into pieces about 5 millimetres (0.2 inches) in size, we then planted them using the tweezers. Once you’ve secured the moss into the soil, the trick to planting it successfully is to hold the moss down with the pick and smoothly pull out the tweezers.

It was difficult at first, but we gradually got the hang of it and eventually succeeded in creating a mossy meadow around the stones. We gave the moss some water, then popped in the figurine we received from our other gacha…

▼ … and then our Capsule Terrarium was complete!

It took about 20 minutes to make, at a leisurely pace, and was incredibly easy to set up. While it was simple to make, it’s also said to be simple to care for too – just give it some water through one of the holes in the top of the capsule about once a fortnight.

With such little care required, we’re confident that anyone could look after a terrarium like this, and after gazing in awe at our creation for around three days, we’re happy to report that it still looks as beautiful as the day we made it. Though there hasn’t been any major growth, that’s to be expected, because depending on the species, moss is said to only grow a few millimetres to around 1 centimetre (0.4 inches) per year.

▼ Part of the appeal of owning a terrarium is being able to slowly watch how it evolves over time.

All this for just 500 yen was a fantastic deal, because usually when you get into terrariums, you have to buy quite a bit upfront to get started. With everything included in the capsule, this was such a great kit that we’re now tempted to pick up a few more on our next trip to Shibuya.

▼ And we might just buy some other little figurines to join our rubber duck while we’re there.

The specialty store has done a great job with the capsule machine, and when we talked to staff about it, they told us that some people get into terarrium gardening after purchasing the capsules, making it a gateway into the world of terrariums.

▼ And there are sooo many beauties to choose from.

So if you’ve always loved the look of terrariums but felt like they might seem difficult to set up and maintain, the gacha terrarium might just help you out. It’s a fun and easy way to enter the world of terrariums on a tiny scale, and it can be purchased online or at Feel the Garden stores around Japan.

title: Heavyweight ramen-style cheese fried chicken bowl appears in Tokyo, but is it genius or madness?
description: Karaage no Tensai invokes the name of Jiro-style ramen, and we head out for a taste test. content:
Karaage no Tensai invokes the name of Jiro-style ramen, and we head out for a taste test.

It’s been said that there’s a fine line between genius and madness, but might that line be deep-fried and covered in cheese? It was the search for the answer to that question that recently led us to downtown Tokyo’s Uguisudani neighborhood.

We were here to visit the local branch of Karaage no Tensai, a restaurant chain whose name translates as “Genius of Fried Chicken.” Part of the Watami restaurant group (most famous for the Watami chain of pubs), Karaage no Tensai opened its first branch in 2018, so it was poised to reap the benefits of the boom in popularity for karaage/Japanese-style fried chicken that took place during the pandemic, when people across the country were looking for hearty comfort food that was takeout-friendly. By the middle of 2021, Karaage no Tensai boasted 100 branches, but these days the chain has dwindled back down to just six locations.

It’s kind of a shame, as Karaage no Tensai’s fried chicken (pictured above) is perfectly tasty stuff. Still, it’s hard to stand out when there’s so much competition in the karaage sphere, which is perhaps what led the Uguisudani branch to take the bold move of offering heavyweight ramen-style cheese karaage rice bowls.

Exclusive to the Uguisudani branch, Karaage no Tensai calls this creation the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don, brazenly invoking the name of the style of ramen popularized by the Ramen Jiro chain, which has no connection to Karaage no Tensai or the Watami group. Jiro-style ramen, for those who haven’t tried it, is characterized by an extra salty and oily broth, copious amounts of garlic, and lots of bean sprouts.

▼ Ramen Jiro ramen

So how does Karaage no Tensai translate this into fried chicken form? Like this.

Visually, the 1,408-yen (US$8.85) Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don definitely makes an impact, with such a large quantity of toppings that they look like they’re about to overflow from the bowl and a surprisingly vivid cheese sauce squirted all across the top.

Starting from the bottom, the bowl is filled with rice, bean sprouts, six nicely sized pieces of karaage, cloves of roasted garlic, and cheese.

The cheese here is kind on an outlier, since it’s not an ingredient you’ll find in Jiro-style ramen. As our taste-testing reporter P.K. Sanjun took a bite, though, the reason for its inclusion became clear. The cheese sauce is strongly salty, and combined with its creaminess, seems to be Karaage no Tensai’s intended facsimile for Jiro-style ramen’s salty, oily broth.

However, the saltiness found in the cheese sauce isn’t present in the other ingredients in the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don, and while the roasted garlic obviously tastes garlicky, P.K. couldn’t detect all that much seasoning to the bean sprouts of fried chicken. As such, salty cheese was the dominant flavor from start to finish, and the taste started to get a little repetitive part-way through the meal, prompting P.K. to munch on a mouthful of bean sprouts from time to time when he found himself wanting a palate cleanser or just a little variety.

All that said, the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don wasn’t a bad meal. It may not actually scratch the Jiro-style ramen itch because of how different the fried chicken bowl ends up being, but it’s still a filling guilty pleasure of a rice bowl, even if it doesn’t really fulfil the promise in its name.

title: A practical guide to freezing your boss’ hat in a block of ice [Photos]
description: This is an important skill for working adults to acquire, and we’re here to walk you through the process step by step. Japan is in the middle of a very hot summer, and it’s got us scrambling to find new ways to keep cool. Earlier in the month we tried slapping 68 cooling patches on […]
content:
This is an important skill for working adults to acquire, and we’re here to walk you through the process step by step.

Japan is in the middle of a very hot summer, and it’s got us scrambling to find new ways to keep cool. Earlier in the month we tried slapping 68 cooling patches on the upper body of our crack reporter Mr. Sato, and while that did provide him with some measure of relief from the heat, we realize that such crazy methods may not be for everyone.

So today we’re going to be testing an alternate crazy method for staying cool this summer: freezing a hat.

Now that we’d decided on our plan, though, we had to answer the question of whose hat to freeze? After giving it some thought, we settled on swiping the hat of SoraNews24 owner and founder Yoshio off of his desk. The decision to give Yoshio this reprieve from the heat was made as a display of employee loyalty and appreciation for our boss’ hard work, and not at all because we weren’t sure if freezing a hat would ruin it and didn’t want to risk our own clothing in this experiment.

So how do you freeze a hat? First, you’re going to need a large bucket or similar container, like the cooking pot we grabbed from the office kitchenette.

Place your boss’ hat inside, upside-down, and stuff a plastic bag inside the hat.

Then fill the container with water…

…and stick it in the freezer.

▼ Eating any unclaimed mango ice cream that happens to be in the freezer is optional.

Exactly how long it’s going to take for the water to freeze will depend on your specific freezer setup, but we let our boss’ hat chill over the weekend, and when we checked on it three days later, that turned out to have been plenty of time.

After setting the pot out to thaw for a bit, we were able to pop the hat out, and it had frozen into a solid block shaped sort of like a curling stone.

Between the solid black color of the fabric and the texturing of the ice, it looked oddly beautiful, like a slab of high-quality polished granite.

However, we had a lot of work left to do before this ice hat would be wearable. Next we heated up some water and very carefully poured it into the plastic bag that we’d placed inside the hat. This melts the ice directly outside the bag without dissolving the other frozen area, clearing out space for the wearer’s head.

However, doing this means that the block of ice loses its uniform shape, and in the process the center of gravity is altered. In order to make this hat something that can be used without sliding off the wearer’s head, we’re going to need to grind off some of the excess ice using a straight file.

This isn’t a quick or easy task, and we felt our arms tiring before we were even close to finishing. Still, you’ll want to work carefully so that you don’t trim off any more ice than you need to.

Making things extra tricky is that while you’re shaving off the part you don’t want, the rest of the ice is going to start thawing. So rather than doing all the trimming and filing in one fell swoop, we needed to complete the process in stages. Once the ice we wanted to keep started seeming like it was in danger of beginning to melt, we put the hat back in the freezer to resolidify, then started filing again the next day.

On Day 2 we also expanded our tool set to include a heated cutter…

…and a heated soup ladle…

…respectively allowing us to make precise cuts or soften up a palm-sized area all at once.

Finally, on the third day of filing/trimming, we were done, and it was time to test whether our boss’ frozen hat would actually make him feel more comfortable.

▼ “Wait, didn’t I leave my hat right here?” asked Yoshio.

▼ Oh, do you mean this hat, boss?

Now, some of you might now be recalling the experiment we previously did in which we froze Yoshio’s glasses, and yes, we did that again this time.

Now reunited with his iced-over belongings, we invited Yoshio to try them out. He started with the hat…

…but when he completed his outfit by slipping on the glasses, the freezing sensation was shockingly intense!

Now, some might say that the proper thing to do here would have been to take these frozen items off. However, Yoshio is always telling us to look for outside-the-box solutions, so instead of removing the sources of pain-inducing cold, we moved Yoshio himself outside, where the chill could be offset by the scorch of direct sunlight.

We walked him to the park near SoraNews24 HQ, which, like a lot of downtown Tokyo’s parks, has some pretty extensive concrete paving which the heat reflects back off of.

Upon arrival, Yoshio could still feel the searingly icy sensation from his glasses’ frozen earpieces on his temples. By comparison, the cooling effects of the frozen hat were slower to manifest, but when they did, they brought on a strong chill at the back and top of his head.

But in time, things started to stabilize, and Yoshio, amazingly, reached a state of comfort.

▼ “Ah, this feels just right.”

▼ “From the neck up, it feels like autumn now.”

So while it’s a time-consuming process, yes, freezing your boss’ hat is an effective way to deal with summer heat. Of course, you could apply this idea to your own hat too, but that would mean missing out on one of the other benefits we were able to reap in our experiment.

Like we said, the cooling effect is so strong as to make the wearer feel uncomfortable in anything but the hottest environment. Should your boss remove his frozen hat while still in the office, though, he’s going to end up with water all over his desk as the ice melts.

So the best plan is to freeze your boss’ hat so that he’ll have to go outside, but won’t be able to come back in until the ice is melted. That way your boss gets to cool off, and you can get your boss out of your hair for a while as he stands thawing in the park.

title: Japanese workers reveal their top five mysterious rules they wish would disappear【Survey】
description: A single vacation can lead to near-forced souvenirs and apologies to the entire office. Japan is world-renowned for its hospitality, respect for tradition, and attention to detail. In Japanese business culture, there’s also a dedication to politeness, where many customs were originally introduced to ensure smooth interactions and avoid conflict. However, as working styles modernize, […]
content:
A single vacation can lead to near-forced souvenirs and apologies to the entire office.

Japan is world-renowned for its hospitality, respect for tradition, and attention to detail. In Japanese business culture, there’s also a dedication to politeness, where many customs were originally introduced to ensure smooth interactions and avoid conflict. However, as working styles modernize, some of these thoughtful gestures have transformed into tiresome daily chores. To see which workplace rules have outlived their usefulness, Tokyo-based media company Mfro (via its Craudia crowdsourcing service) surveyed 493 working adults, 366 women and 127 men ranging from their 20s to 50s and older.

The top five mysterious workplace manners that Japanese employees secretly wish would disappear are:

5. Mandatory souvenir sharing (4.7 percent)

Bringing back local snacks (omiyage) for co-workers after a vacation or business trip is a way to share experiences and show gratitude, but when employees feel pressured to spend extra time and money hunting down treats, it becomes less of a thoughtful gift and more of a chore.

▼ “I heard you went to Okinawa. Where are the snacks?”

4. Excessive greetings (9.1 percent)

For anyone who has studied even just the basics of the language, you’ll know that polite greetings are the bedrock of Japanese communication. However, some offices take this to extreme levels that actually put a halt to productivity. These offices require staff to walk around the entire floor or department to greet every coworker individually upon arriving or leaving, or physically stand up at their desks whenever an executive enters the room.

3. Over-the-top chat messaging (11 percent)

Messaging apps like Slack, Line, and Teams are intended to speed up communication in the office, and yet traditional corporate etiquette has managed to sneak right into the group chats. Instead of quick, informal updates, workers feel forced to start every single message with long, formal greetings when sometimes a simple emoji reaction would wrap up the conversation effectively.

2. Vacation apologies and snacks (15.4 percent)

Paid leave is a legal right, but in a culture heavily focused on the collective team and the business instead of the individual, taking time off can leave workers feeling guilty about passing their workload to their teammates. Before taking a planned day off, employees might have to announce it to the entire office during morning meetings and, upon returning, they often feel obligated to go desk-to-desk apologizing for their absence and distributing snacks, even though they didn’t technically do anything wrong.

1. Rigid email etiquette (21.5 percent)

Japanese business emails are notoriously formal, requiring elaborate standard set phrases and seasonal blessings, and some offices even insist on listing all internal email recipients in strict order of corporate seniority, which feels like it’s wasting precious extra minutes that could be spent on real work.

▼ “Should I be using ‘intense heat season’ (酷暑の候, kokusho no ko) or ‘lingering heat season’ (残暑の候, zansho no ko) here?”

When asked about the biggest stress caused by these rules, 35.3 percent of respondents said it was “mental fatigue”, followed by taking up time (27.0 percent) and taking extra effort (26.6 percent).

Even if a significant portion of employees find the rules exhausting, it’s not as simple as just deciding to stop following them. The primary reason for not stopping was that they fear what others will think (36.1 percent), followed closely by the fact that it has already become the default norm (32.9 percent). In group-oriented work dynamics, stepping out of line risks making coworkers and your boss think you are rude or uncooperative. Among the respondents, some did mention that they had quit these mysterious manners, but are now looked at strangely by others at the office due to it.

So, these mysterious customs are more of a product of peer pressure and the traditional office environment, rather than being driven by pure logic. As remote work grows and generational turnover occurs, office atmospheres could potentially shift naturally, and these unwritten rules could slowly fade out of existence. However, to truly tackle these issues, the leadership needs to step in, recognize these problems, and create safe environments for employees to voice discomfort without the fear of social friction.

title: These Japanese contact lenses let you put anime characters on your eyes [Photos]
description: Chiikawa contacts are a cute way to add some subtle anime flair to your look. In Japanese, there’s a phrase, “Me ni irete mo itakunai,” which translates literally to “It won’t hurt even if you put it into your eye.” What could be so wonderous that you wouldn’t mind doing something ordinarily so painful? Why, […]
content:
Chiikawa contacts are a cute way to add some subtle anime flair to your look.

In Japanese, there’s a phrase, “Me ni irete mo itakunai,” which translates literally to “It won’t hurt even if you put it into your eye.” What could be so wonderous that you wouldn’t mind doing something ordinarily so painful? Why, something very, very cute, of course!

Me in irete mo itakunai is most commonly used by people to describe their children, grandchildren, or pets, but if we’re talking about cute things, we can’t forget about the anime/manga character Chiikawa, whose very name is a contraction of the words chiisai (“small”) and kawaii (“cute”). So today we’re going to be putting the compactly adorable Chiikawa into our eye…or at least onto it.

Allowing us to do this is En Giorno, a brand of contact lenses from Japanese cosmetics and merchandising company Shobido. En Giorno’s Chiikawa collaboration lineup consists of four models, Chiikawa Pink, Hachiware Greige, Usagi Brown, and Momonga Gray.

We opted to try out the Chiikawa Pink version, and naturally the character is featured on the packaging. There’s more to this crossover than that though, because Chiikawa is also on the contact lenses themselves!

Wasting no time, our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo promptly put Chiikawa onto her eye, and just like the saying had assured us, it didn’t hurt at all, though that probably has more to do with En Giorno’s precision manufacturing methods than the character’s cuteness.

Still, these lenses are indeed cute, and even more so than Natsuki had at first expected. It wasn’t until she had them in that she noticed that Chiikawa is surrounded by some illustrated sparkles, adding yet another dose of manga-aesthetic style to your eyes.

With the Chiikawa contacts in, Natsuki was looking forward to the excited reactions of friends and family throughout the day. Things didn’t unfold exactly as she’d expected them to, though, since no one, on their own, noticed her new ocular occupant.

This is, perhaps, something we should have seen coming. The En Giorno Chiikawa illustration really does follow the directives of both parts of the character’s name, as it’s very cute, but also very small.

▼ The Chiikawa contact lenses next to a Sylvanian Families baby plushie, the international scientific community’s widely accepted standard for scale comparisons.

On the other hand, every single person who Natsuki pointed out the Chiikawa illustrations instantly got a burst of giddy excitement from the revelation, and actually, the subtle size is probably a plus. For one thing, the illustration is compact enough that it doesn’t affect the wearer’s field of vision, and since it doesn’t immediately stand out, these lenses are pieces of Chiikawa flair that you can wear without disrupting your overall look.

▼ The En Giorno Chiikawa contact lenses come in both prescription and non-prescription versions, and are priced at 2,200 yen (US$14) a pair on the Shobido online store, Amazon, and Rakuten.

So while they’d be an apt choice for a meetup with fellow fans or when heading out to a Chiikawa event or anime screening, they’re also something you can use when just going about your daily life, so that if and when you do run into something unpleasant during the day, you can tell yourself “It’s OK, I’ve got Chiikawa with me.”

title: Time-lapse footage shows just how fast rebuilding in Kumamoto can go
description: All in a day’s work. Whenever major natural disasters hit Japan, I’m always amazed by the engineering feats that were set up in various places to minimize casualties and damage. It’s hard to feel a sense of joy or pride at times like the 7.1 magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto recently, but at the same […]
content:
All in a day’s work.

Whenever major natural disasters hit Japan, I’m always amazed by the engineering feats that were set up in various places to minimize casualties and damage. It’s hard to feel a sense of joy or pride at times like the 7.1 magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto recently, but at the same time it feels like a lot of hard work and ingenuity that goes into damage prevention often gets overlooked.

One prime example I noticed in the immediate aftermath was scenes of elevated highways sheared into two completely disjoined sections. It was constantly played on a loop as a symbol of the catastrophic power of the earthquake without any explanation as to why the roads looked like that.

▼ It was basically the exploded AEON Mall, broken smokestack, and broken highway, over and over again for the first day.

The highways were designed to break like that in the event of an earthquake to prevent even bigger devastation. If the entire overpass was one solid unit, one weakened section would cause the entire structure to fall down, as happened in the 1995 Awaji-Hanshin earthquake.

▼ A news report in the aftermath of the Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake showing the massive destruction of elevated expressways. In the latter part, Prof. Fukuwa explains that the flaw in the design was using combinations of materials that vibrated at different frequencies together in a rigid structure.

The news footage seldom, if ever, showed what was going on underneath those detached segments, which is where the real magic happens. Systems can vary as needed, but often these cables, rods, and stoppers not only reduce overall damage but make repairs easier and faster.

▼ This video is in Japanese, but the images alone should demonstrate how well-thought-out these mechanisms are, built on lessons learned from past disasters.

And speaking of fast repairs, with earthquakes an ever-present threat, crews are well-trained to react to damage quickly and thoroughly. A good example of this can be seen in a time-lapse video of a highway repair in Kumamoto done by workers for NEXCO, Japan’s privatized company that manages the nation’s expressways.

▼ “We are currently doing reconstruction work on the southbound/outbound lane of the Katanogawa Bridge along the Kyushu Expressway, after it was damaged in the 2026 Kumamoto Earthquake. This video shows the asphalt work in progress. The entire team is working in close coordination, prioritizing safety above all else. We will keep on working toward a fast recovery.”

令和８年熊本地震により損傷した九州自動車道　片野川橋（下り線）の復旧作業を行っております。
動画は、アスファルト舗装の実施状況です。
工事関係者が一丸となり、緊密に連携を図りながら、安全を最優先に工事に取り組んでおります。
引き続き、早期復旧に向けて着実に工事を進めてまいります。… pic.twitter.com/RnlYfZX9aU

— 【公式】NEXCO西日本 (@w_nexco_news) August 9, 2026

In the video, a stretch of collapsed and heavily crumpled road on the Katanogawa Bridge becomes a pristine sheet of asphalt in seconds, which in real time was about 10 hours, but still extremely efficient. Unfortunately, the speed also makes it hard to see all the work that goes into rebuilding the underlaying structure of the road in addition to repaving it.

It’s also worth noting that the date on the video is 8 August, the Saturday kicking off the national holiday period known as Obon, where a lot of people take off work and relax. That combined with the overall heat of a Japanese summer would make roadwork a particularly grueling experience. Comments online were full of respect for those workers, with wishes that they stay safe and get a fat paycheck at the end of all this.

“Seriously incredible! Thank you for your hard work in this intense heat and during the holidays.”
“They did that in 10 hours?!”
“That’s fantastic to see. Truly supporting the arteries of Japan, and you can sense the pride in their work.”
“I hope they’re all given big fat bonuses for that.”
“I used to work in asphalt, and I have a huge amount of respect for people who work under that heat and those tight safety conditions. I hope they stay safe.”
“It’s sad that politicians get paid more than those people.”
“I wish they could do normal road construction that fast.”
“But after doing it so fast, is it safe to use?”

I’m going to go out on a limb and say that if any corners were cut and safety regulations were ignored in this particular project, NEXCO wouldn’t post incriminating evidence of it for all the world to see online. Then again, I’m not a marketing expert. Maybe that’s the cool thing for companies to do on social media nowadays.

It’s just good to see things are getting better there bit by bit, and people’s ability to prepare for, prevent, and recover from disasters here remains something to be admired.

title: Japan’s Rabbit Island in danger of becoming Boar Island, tourists asked to follow feeding rules
description: One of the cutest places in Japan needs visitors’ help keeping rabbit food, and rabbits themselves, from becoming boar food. There’s an island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea called Okunoshima. Written with the kanji 大久野島, Okunoshima’s name translates roughly to “Island with a Field from Long Ago,” which, to be honest, is a description you […]
content:
One of the cutest places in Japan needs visitors’ help keeping rabbit food, and rabbits themselves, from becoming boar food.

There’s an island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea called Okunoshima. Written with the kanji 大久野島, Okunoshima’s name translates roughly to “Island with a Field from Long Ago,” which, to be honest, is a description you could apply to a lot of places in Japan. However, Okunoshima’s nickname is much more specifically descriptive: Rabbit Island.

Okunoshima has no permanent human residents, but the island is now home to more than 500 wild rabbits. Rabbits aren’t indigenous to the island, but were introduced to the environment sometime in the 1970s, with one theory being that the initial group was brought in by visiting children who’d raised the animals at their school and then set them loose on the island.

Regardless of how they got there, the Okunoshima bunnies got to doing what bunnies do, and the population grew to the point that pretty much as soon as you arrive in port, you’re going to spot wild rabbits who aren’t at all shy around human visitors. The little guys have no qualms about sauntering up to people in expectation of snacks, and many, if not most, visitors can be seen carrying around bags of chopped vegetables, either purchased from vendors on the island or brought from home, to feed the rabbits.

However, in recent years researchers have noticed some concerning changes in the ecosystem, and if not kept in check, there’s a risk of Rabbit Island turning into Wild Boar Island.

Like rabbits, boars aren’t native to Okunoshima, but researchers started noticing them on the island around 15 years ago, and have confirmed that they’ve bred on Okunoshima since then. The prevailing theory is that the boars swam over from the neighboring island of Omishima, based on reports from locals who say they witnessed such crossings.

▼ There is ferry service between Omishima and Okunoshima, but historically wild boars have been unable to surmount the challenges of navigating the reservation and payment systems.

Boars are not particularly picky eaters, and researchers believe that they’ve developed a habit of eating excess food that Okunoshima visitors leave for the rabbits. Basically, visitors, either because the bunnies are just so gosh darn cute or because they’re in a rush because they’ve got a ferry home to catch, have been putting out more food than the rabbits actually consume, but the boars are happy to chow down on the leftovers.

While this pattern is, technically, eliminating food waste, as a result of being well-fed the island’s boar population is increasing. This creates a risk of disrupting the ecological balance, and in recent years researchers from Fukushima University and the National Institute of Technology’s Kure College have confirmed cases of boars attacking rabbits on the island. There’s also the possibility that boars, which can exhibit aggressive or destructive behavior, could begin causing harm to human visitors or the island’s infrastructure.

Though attacks on rabbits appear to still be at an isolated-incident level of frequency, culling of boars via box traps is periodically carried out on Okunoshima. The preferable way for the situation to be handled, though, would be to not supply the boars with extra food to facilitate breeding. Since at least 2024, the joint committee created by the Ministry of Environment and the local tourism board have been asking that visitors who put out food wait and watch as the rabbits eat it. Should the rabbits not eat all of the food, visitors are asked to pick up any leftover portion to take home or otherwise dispose of in a proper garbage receptacle, so that it doesn’t become dinner for the boars. The committee is now once again calling for visitors to be conscious of the amount of food they set out and refrain from doing things such as dumping out the remnants of their bags in a pile before hopping on the ferry home, and hopefully travelers will comply so that the island doesn’t have to ban feeding the rabbits altogether.

title: Stay at a hotel with a bed for your plushie in Japan
description: Complete with tiny matching pyjamas for your little friend. The world of fandom is vast and varied in Japan – on one hand you have fans who might show a casual interest in an actor, idol, VTuber, or anime character, and then on the other, you have diehard fans who engage in what’s known as […]
content:
Complete with tiny matching pyjamas for your little friend.

The world of fandom is vast and varied in Japan – on one hand you have fans who might show a casual interest in an actor, idol, VTuber, or anime character, and then on the other, you have diehard fans who engage in what’s known as “oshi-katsu”. Equivalent to the English slang term “stanning” – katsu means “activities” while oshi refers to the character or person you’re “stanning” – this level of fandom is reserved for those who go to great lengths to support the object of their affections at any given opportunity, investing time, effort and money into the activity, and treating it like a passionate pasttime.

One of the ways to show your love in the oshi-katsu world is by buying merch dedicated to your favourite idol or character, often in the form of a plushie, known as “nuigurumi” (“nui” for short) in Japanese. Nuigurumi are great for snuggling up to at night, and you can even take them out on trips with you, both near and far. It’s a passion that Japanese business hotel chain Toyoko Inn clearly understands, as it’s been officially catering to guests and their plushies since autumn 2025, when it started the “Oshi-Katsu Support Plan”.

A lot of fans would have stayed at Toyoko Inn for oshi events and concerts, so it’s a clever idea to create an accommodation plan geared towards them. There are actually two types of Oshi-Katsu Support Plans offered by Toyoko Inn – one is the “Relax & Recharge – Oshi Edition”, which comes with a free pack of foot care sheets, bath salts, and a heated eye mask to help you “unwind after a day of oshi-katsu”, while the other is the “Oshi-Katsu Sleepover Plan – Stay with Your Favorite Plushie!”, which gives you and your nui separate beds in the same room for the night.

▼ The stay is ideal for acrylic standees too, as this poster at the front desk reads: “We’ve started renting beds for plushies and acrylic stands.”

Our own reporter Maro, who has a few nuis of her own, was excited to try the Sleepover Plan, and when she learned that her plushie’s stay would cost a meagre 300 yen (US$1.88) on top of her room fee, she felt so heartened by the customer service that she packed several of her favourite plushies to join her on the sleepover.

Booking a stay for her and her plushie was a unique experience in itself, but when she got to the front desk, she was even more delighted when staff handed her a mesh bag at check-in, containing bedding and nightwear for her plush character.

While the stay is generally designed for one plushie, you could take several and let them share or rotate during your stay. The set contains a duvet, a pillow, a bed frame and nightwear in two sizes, though, so if you take more than two plushies, they won’t all be able to wear matching outfits.

As for where to put the bedding in your room, it fits perfectly into the curved space where you might normally put your smartphone and other small items when you go to sleep.

▼ The idea to repurpose this design feature into a toy bed is a work of genius.

Excited to give her nui the hotel experience, Maro took out the nightwear for her plushie. The nightwear gowns come in two sizes, small and large, and they have Velcro on the back, so they can be made to work with nuis, or standees, of various sizes.

Maro’s main nui has a rather large head, so the nightwear was bursting at the seams a little. The outfit would be more suitable for a regular human-shaped nui, but it still worked on her character plush, so it really does suit a wide variety of shapes and sizes.

Another cute feature is how the tiny nightwear matches the larger one designed to be used by human guests. Cue photos of you and your nui in matching nightwear during your hotel stay.

Though the nightwear required a bit of fiddling, due to the odd shape of her plushie, the bed slid into the space with ease. Within seconds, Maro had made the bed, and when she stood back to admire her work, she was impressed by how good it looked in the light.

▼ A tiny nook for your nui!

▼ Two nuis can fit in the bed if you rearrange their sleeping positions.

The space looked so good it was like it had been designed specifically for a nui bed, and the fun of the special accommodation plan doesn’t end there – if you post a photo or video of yourself using the plan on social media, you can also receive a “small gift”. Maro couldn’t find any information online about what the gift might entail, so she went ahead and snapped a photo of her nui looking as cosy as a bug in a rug.

[twitter https://twitter.com/hironamaro/status/2080639034653880681 align=”center”]

After sharing the photo on Twitter and showing it to staff at the front desk, Maro received…

▼… a toothbrush case set!

While the set doesn’t include a toothbrush – just the case and toothpaste – it’s an exclusive item that comes with a cute illustration on the front, making it as stylish as it is practical. She didn’t expect to get something so substantial in return for her social media post, so she was overjoyed by her free small gift.

▼ Her other plushie looked pretty happy about it too.

Looking into it further, Maro discovered that the toothbrush set is actually made from recycled plastic, sourced from used plastic toothbrushes and combs that are collected from Toyoko Inn hotels nationwide.

▼ Pop your used combs and toothbrushes in this receptacle in the bathroom, and you’ll be giving them a new life.

If you’re yet to discover the world of oshi-katsu, this type of customer service might seem a little mind-boggling, but for fans who go all out for their beloved characters and idols, it’s a dream service that makes for a very memorable stay. Even if you’re not into oshi-katsu, it’s a fun plan for guests with children who have plush toys that are like family members, and you’d be hard-pressed to find anything like it at any other hotel chain.

While no end date has been announced for the plan itself, the free-gift social media campaign runs until 31 August. So if you’ve ever dreamed of treating your plushie to a hotel experience that would make other plushies envious, now’s the time to book a getaway at the inn.

title: 12-year-old British girl who went missing in Tokyo found safe after visiting anime sites around Yokohama
description: Police say she also spent time at an Internet cafe. Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old British secondary school student who went missing while travelling in Japan with her family, has been found safe after spending time at an Internet cafe while visiting anime-related locations around Yokohama. Carmelita had been staying with her family at a […]
content:
Police say she also spent time at an Internet cafe.

Carmelita Lakdesha Paul, a 12-year-old British secondary school student who went missing while travelling in Japan with her family, has been found safe after spending time at an Internet cafe while visiting anime-related locations around Yokohama.

Carmelita had been staying with her family at a private rental property in Minami-Kamata, a neighbourhood in Tokyo’s Ota Ward, after arriving in Japan for sightseeing with her parents and older brother on 21 July. She was reported missing by her mother shortly before 9:30 a.m. on 13 August, after the family awoke at around 8:30 a.m. and realised she was gone.

The Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department issued a public request for information the following day, and officers continued searching for Carmelita, including checking security camera footage. Through surveillance footage, they were able to trace her whereabouts to Yokohama Station in Tokyo’s neighbouring Kanagawa Prefecture on the morning of her disappearance but they were unable to locate her beyond that. Carmelita was said to only have a few thousand yen (less than US$100) on her when she left, and she did not take her passport with her.

▼ The train journey between Keikyu-Kamata, the nearest station to the vacation rental, and Yokohama takes around 12 minutes.

At around 8 p.m. on 15 August, roughly 59 hours after she left the family’s accommodation, Carmelita walked into a police box in Yokohama by herself. She was unharmed and reportedly told officers that she had begun to miss her parents.

Police say Carmelita had gone out to visit anime “pilgrimage sites” (the term used to describe real-world locations associated with an anime or manga) and had also stayed at an Internet cafe.

Although police haven’t released details of how long she stayed at the Internet cafe, this part of the story raises questions about how a 12-year-old was able to stay there. Although entry for people under 18 is generally permitted during daytime hours, there are late-night restrictions for minors, even those accompanied by a parent or guardian, so it remains unclear how long she stayed there and under what conditions.

While police haven’t revealed any other details, except to say they do not believe any crime occurred, additional details about Carmelita’s movements were provided by Tsunehiko Maeda, a former prosecutor, in an online comment.

Maeda said that the day before Carmelita went missing, she had told her parents that she wanted to visit Yokohama to see locations associated with Bungo Stray Dogs, an anime that she likes. He also said investigators found evidence that she had travelled from Keikyu Kamata Station to Yokohama Station using a transport IC card and she was due to return to her home country with her family on the day of her disappearance.

Bungo Stray Dogs, the anime that reportedly inspired Carmelita’s trip to Yokohama, is set largely in Yokohama and follows the members of the Armed Detective Agency, a group of detectives with supernatural abilities. It won’t be lost on fans of the anime that after spending two nights away from her family while visiting locations associated with the series, Carmelita found herself seeking help from the real-life police there.

With police saying there was no criminal involvement in the disappearance, Carmelita has now been safely reunited with her family.

Sources: Yomiuri, Asahi Shimbun,  FNN via Yahoo! News Japan

description: There’s a manga-related reason Inunakin is so buff.
